Here it tells you at a glance that the right-hand third of both panels is drawn over very little data, which is the point the whole previous section had to make with a table.

```{r pp-and-me}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"
#| label: fig-ppme
#| fig-cap: "Two marginal effects of democracy from the same model. Left: the average derivative, the change in Pr(dispute) per one-point move in democracy. Right: the average discrete change over the full range of democracy. Both at each value of the capability ratio, with delta-method intervals."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels against the logged capability ratio. The left panel shows the average derivative of dispute probability with respect to democracy, rising from about minus 0.008 toward zero and flattening out just above it. The right panel shows the discrete change over the full democracy range, rising from about minus 0.11 on the same shape. Both have confidence bands that widen to the right, and in both the band still includes zero everywhere past the crossing point. A rug along the bottom shows the data thinning out to the right."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5

cr_grid <- seq(0, 9, 0.1)          # capability ratios to evaluate at

# ---- PANEL A: average marginal effect of democracy (a derivative) -----------
ame_est <- numeric(length(cr_grid))
ame_se  <- numeric(length(cr_grid))

for (i in seq_along(cr_grid)) {

  Xi <- X2                                              # counterfactual COPY
  Xi[, "lncaprat"]      <- cr_grid[i]                   # this capability ratio, every dyad
  Xi[, "deml:lncaprat"] <- Xi[, "deml"] * cr_grid[i]    # product tracks BOTH columns
  # deml is deliberately NOT set. Every dyad keeps its own democracy score, which
  # is what makes this an AVERAGE marginal effect rather than the effect at some
  # constructed democracy value.

  p     <- plogis(as.vector(Xi %*% b2))                 # n predicted probabilities
  slope <- b2["deml"] + cr_grid[i] * b2["deml:lncaprat"]  # effect on the LOG-ODDS

  ame_est[i] <- mean(p * (1 - p)) * slope               # weight each case, then average

  # delta gradient: the estimate is mean(weight) x slope, and beta moves both
  g <- colMeans(p * (1 - p) * (1 - 2 * p) * Xi) * slope
  g["deml"]          <- g["deml"] + mean(p * (1 - p))
  g["deml:lncaprat"] <- g["deml:lncaprat"] + mean(p * (1 - p)) * cr_grid[i]
  ame_se[i] <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(g) %*% V2 %*% g))
}

# ---- PANEL B: average discrete change, democracy from -10 to +10 -----------
dd_est <- numeric(length(cr_grid))
dd_sd  <- numeric(length(cr_grid))

for (i in seq_along(cr_grid)) {

  Xlo <- X2                                             # two counterfactual COPIES
  Xhi <- X2
  Xlo[, "lncaprat"]      <- cr_grid[i]                  # same capability ratio in both
  Xhi[, "lncaprat"]      <- cr_grid[i]
  Xlo[, "deml"]          <- -10                         # fully autocratic
  Xhi[, "deml"]          <-  10                         # fully democratic
  Xlo[, "deml:lncaprat"] <- -10 * cr_grid[i]            # products track both columns
  Xhi[, "deml:lncaprat"] <-  10 * cr_grid[i]

  plo <- plogis(as.vector(Xlo %*% b2))                  # n predictions at deml = -10
  phi <- plogis(as.vector(Xhi %*% b2))                  # n predictions at deml = +10

  dd_est[i] <- mean(phi - plo)                          # average the n differences

  g <- colMeans(phi * (1 - phi) * Xhi) - colMeans(plo * (1 - plo) * Xlo)
  dd_sd[i] <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(g) %*% V2 %*% g))
}

me_d <- tibble(lncaprat = cr_grid, est = ame_est, se = ame_se,
               panel = "A. Derivative: per one-point move")
me_c <- tibble(lncaprat = cr_grid, est = dd_est,  se = dd_sd,
               panel = "B. Discrete: full -10 to +10 move")

me_panel <- function(d) d %>%
  mutate(lo = est - 1.96 * se, hi = est + 1.96 * se) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = lncaprat, y = est)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = bu_palegreen, alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = bu_grey) +
  geom_rug(data = slice_sample(dp, n = 1500), aes(x = lncaprat), inherit.aes = FALSE,
           alpha = 0.15, color = bu_grey) +
  labs(title = unique(d$panel), x = "ln(capability ratio)", y = "change in Pr(dispute)") +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = bu_grey, fill = NA, linewidth = 0.3))

me_panel(me_d) | me_panel(me_c)
```

In either panel, the finding is that becoming more democratic reduces the chances of conflict for dyads at parity, but has little or no effect for dyads with imbalances. Put differently, the marginal effect of an increase in democracy is to decrease the chances of conflict across the range of capabilities, but that dampening effect gets smaller as capability ratios get larger. By the time ln(capabilities) reaches about 5, democracy exerts no measurable effect on conflict. 

Panel B is a better one for these data - it's differenced and set up between the cases where Polity is -10 and +10. We can say something explicit about the change in $x$ here, and the effects are on a more meaningful scale because of the large change in $x$. The marginal effect of moving from -10 to +10 on Polity for a dyad at parity is to reduce the chances of conflict by about 8 percentage points. Again, because Polity is discrete, this is a marginally more appropriate method, though you can see in the figures it really doesn't matter. 

Compare these to the predicted probabilities and you'll see they tell the same basic story. In @fig-pp, reading left-to-right, you can see the probability of conflict for a dyad at parity declines over the range of democracy from about 9.5% to something close to zero. In @fig-ppme, reading just at the left side, for dyads at parity, an increase in democracy is associated with a decrease of about 8 percentage points in the chance of conflict. These are just different ways to represent and discuss conditional effects.

# Include a multiplicative interaction or not? 

My view is conditionally with Rainey. **If you have an explicit conditional expectation, state it and measure it** — write the multiplicative interaction and test it. A conditional claim deserves a parameter of its own, and leaning on curvature to carry an argument you could have specified is a bad trade.

If you *don't* have a conditional expectation, it is still reasonable, and I'd argue desirable, to look at the effect of your variable of interest at several values of an interesting control. That is common practice and usually good practice. You are describing what your model implies, which is what interpretation is for, and you will frequently learn something.

**But don't label it.** Do not write "compression" or "inherent interaction" in a paper. The label adds nothing to the interpretation — the effects are the effects either way — and it will needlessly earn you a reviewer who does not know this literature saying *wait a minute, I don't see an interaction in your table*. You will then spend a response letter explaining link functions to somebody who did not ask. Report the effect of $x_1$ at several values of the control, describe what you find, and leave this fairly rarified vocabulary out of it.



# Take away points

1. **Nonlinear models are interactive in all of their variables.** The marginal effect is $\lambda(x\beta)\beta_k$, the weight depends on every covariate, so the effect of $x_1$ depends on $x_2$ with no product term anywhere. This is compression.
2. **On the curve, a dummy is an intercept shift, and that is the whole story.** Sliding $x\beta$ by a constant buys different amounts of probability depending on how steep the curve is where you land. A product term does something the shift cannot — it changes the slope, so the two group curves are no longer the same curve in two places, and their difference can grow, move, or change sign.
3. **Compression is not your theory.** It is a fixed shape — effects biggest near $Pr = 0.5$, shrinking toward both tails — that the link imposes. It cannot change a sign, and it cannot represent a conditional claim that is not about curvature.
4. **So a null product term does not mean "no interaction."** In the democratic peace model democracy's effect is two and a half times larger among contiguous dyads, and the product term testing exactly that is nowhere near significant.
5. **Specify the interaction your theory claims, and test it.** Then report *effects* at meaningful values of the moderator, with the conditional standard error that includes the covariance term — not the coefficients.
6. **Interpret this way; don't *name* it this way.** Looking at the effect of $x_1$ at several values of an interesting control is common and usually good practice, with or without a product term. Calling it "compression" or "inherent interaction" in a manuscript adds nothing to the interpretation and earns you a reviewer who says they don't see an interaction in your table.
7. **Check the two assumptions nobody checks.** Plot the binned effects against the line your product term drew, and put a histogram of the moderator under every conditional-effect plot. A sign change out where there is no data is not a finding.
8. **Say which quantity you are reporting and why.** Logit-scale conditional effects are straight lines by construction; probability-scale effects carry compression too, and they are what your hypothesis was about.
9. **Plot the predicted probabilities before you plot the effects.** An effect is a distance between two of them — the gap between group curves, or the slope of one. Levels let a reader judge whether a difference is big; a difference on its own does not.
10. **Ask whether the counterfactual exists before you ask whether it is precise.** A conditional-effect plot draws a line at every value of the moderator whether or not cases live there, and the shape you imposed decides what it says out in the empty region. Here that manufactured a sign change the data do not support.
